Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette:
David, a distinguished 59-year-old professor of history, sought help after decades of quietly managing an internal landscape dominated by a persistent, gnawing dread. He presented as a thoughtful, articulate man, yet his posture held a subtle tension, and his eyes frequently scanned the room, betraying a deep-seated unease. His single status, he admitted, was less a choice and more a consequence of a life increasingly circumscribed by an event that had unfolded forty years prior during Hurricane Agnes. David, then a young man, had been desperately trying to secure their family home in rural North Carolina as the floodwaters rose with terrifying speed. His younger brother, Michael, had been trapped in the basement when the retaining wall buckled, unleashing a torrent of muddy, foul-smelling water. Despite David’s frantic efforts, the current was too strong, the water too deep, and the reek of damp earth and sewage too overwhelming. He remembered the horror of Michael’s last, terrified scream, swallowed by the roar of the flood.

Since that day, the world had become a minefield of potential threats for David. A sudden downpour outside his office window, the kind that made the campus drains gurgle loudly, would instantly seize him. Before David could even consciously register the sound, his body would react, a primal jolt of terror shooting through him. His heart would pound, his breath would quicken, and a wave of intense fear and horror would wash over him, leaving him utterly unable to relax, even in the familiar safety of his university office. This visceral response, where his body reacted to danger before his mind had time to think, was exhausting. It wasn't just visual cues; the faint, earthy smell of wet leaves after a rainstorm, or the distinctive scent of stagnant water near a campus pond, could also trigger this cascade of overwhelming negative emotions – the same terror and guilt he felt watching the flood claim Michael.

This persistent state of internal alarm, the feeling that his body was always poised for danger, had a perverse effect. It made him acutely sensitive to anything that might hint at a threat. He found himself unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, constantly scanning his environment for any sign of water or dampness. The general stress of his demanding academic career, once manageable, now became a trigger in itself. When deadlines loomed or administrative pressures mounted, his already elevated threat response would intensify, making him perceive even innocuous sounds or smells as potential harbingers of the terror he so desperately sought to avoid. He was certain that his internal state of agitation was making him more vulnerable, drawing the very triggers he feared towards him.

Over the years, David had developed elaborate strategies to manage this constant internal pressure. He meticulously checked weather forecasts, avoided routes that took him near rivers or large bodies of water, and even adjusted his lecture schedule to avoid teaching in buildings with known plumbing issues or near campus fountains. He declined invitations to conferences in coastal cities, explaining it away as a preference for drier climates, though the truth was the omnipresent threat of water felt unbearable. This meant missing out on valuable networking and research opportunities, slowly isolating him from his peers. The constant vigilance, the inability to ever truly let his guard down, had left him with a pervasive sense of exhaustion and a deep, unshakeable sadness. He carried the burden of guilt, believing he had failed Michael, and this conviction fueled his inability to find peace.

What finally brought David to seek help was a particularly harrowing incident during a recent campus flood drill. Though it was only a simulated event, the sight of students evacuating and the blare of the alarms had sent him spiraling into such a profound state of panic that he had been unable to teach for days. He was tired of his body reacting before his mind, tired of the unrelenting fear and horror, and profoundly weary of living a life where true relaxation felt like an impossible dream. He hoped, desperately, that someone could help him untangle the decades-old knot of terror and grief that still held him captive.
